subject: system-design
title: Caching
summary: Where caches live, how to read and write through them, eviction, invalidation, HTTP caching, distributed caches and the failure modes that take systems down.

lessons.title: Choose workloads that benefit from caching
lessons.summary: Explain reuse, latency and backend-load savings, then decide when cached copies are appropriate.
lessons.body:
A **cache** is a small, fast store that keeps copies of data that lives somewhere slower or more expensive. You put one in front of a source of truth so that repeated requests for the same thing don't pay the full cost every time.

Caching helps when a workload has reuse or skew. Some workloads approximate a Zipf-like popularity pattern, but a fixed 80/20 split is not universal; measure the actual access distribution. In workloads with temporal locality, a value read once is likely to be read again soon. This is called **locality of reference**: temporal locality (the same item again) and spatial locality (nearby items).

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: the kitchen worktop
> A cook keeps oil, spices and a favourite knife on the worktop and everything else in the cupboards or at the shop. The worktop is small, but most reaches land on it because the same few things are used again and again.
>
> **How it maps:** The worktop is the cache, the cupboards and shop are the slower source of truth, and "the same few things used again and again" is skew plus temporal locality. A small worktop works only because use is concentrated.
>
> **Where it stops:** The oil on the worktop is the real oil, not a copy. A cache holds copies, so the original can change while the copy stays the same (staleness), and wiping the cache should cost only speed, never data.

## What a cache buys you

There are three separate benefits, and it helps to know which one you are after.

- **Lower latency.** Reading a nearby copy from memory skips the backend's own work (a query, a page render, a remote API call) and often a network trip too. How much time that saves depends on your hardware, payload and load, so measure it rather than trusting a generic latency table.
- **Less load on the backend.** Every hit is a request your database never sees. A 95% hit ratio means the database handles 1 in 20 reads.
- **Lower cost.** Serving bytes from a CDN edge or from RAM is often far cheaper than recomputing a page or paying for database capacity.

The price you pay is **staleness** and **complexity**. A cache holds a copy, and copies can disagree with the original. Most of this module is about managing that cost.

> [!note] A cache is not a database
> Treat cached data as disposable. If the cache is wiped, the system should get slower, not wrong. If losing the cache loses data, you have built a database without a database's guarantees.

### Is caching worth it here?

A cache helps when:

1. Reads greatly outnumber writes for the same key.
2. The same keys are requested repeatedly (skewed access).
3. Slightly stale data is acceptable, or you can invalidate reliably.
4. The value is expensive to produce: a slow query, an aggregation, a rendered page, a remote API call.

A cache helps little or hurts when every request is for a different key (a long-tail scan), when data changes on almost every read, or when correctness requires the very latest value (a bank balance used to authorise a payment).

> [!warning] Misses can cost more than no cache
> A miss pays the cache round trip *plus* the backend. If your hit ratio is very low, you have added latency and a new failure point for almost no benefit.

## Key takeaways
- Reuse and skew let a small cache answer a large share of reads; measure the actual access distribution.
- Caching trades lower latency, backend work and cost for stale copies and more moving parts.
- Keep disposable copies in caches; payment authorisation and other correctness decisions still need authoritative checks.

## Further reading
- [Caching overview — AWS](https://aws.amazon.com/caching/)
- [Locality of reference — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Locality_of_reference)
- [Cache (computing) — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cache_(computing))

questions.prompt: Why does a cache that holds only 10% of all keys often achieve a hit ratio well above 10%?

options.text: Because caches compress data, so 10% of the memory holds far more than 10% of the keys
options.explanation: Compression may help memory use, but the premise says the cache holds 10% of the keys. The hit ratio is about which keys are requested, not how they are stored.

options.text: Because every miss automatically loads all neighbouring keys into the cache
options.explanation: Pre-fetching neighbours (spatial locality) is used in CPU caches and some databases, but it is not an automatic property of application caches and does not explain the general effect.

options.text: Because the hit ratio counts writes as hits
options.explanation: Hit ratio is defined over lookups: hits divided by hits plus misses. Writes are not counted as hits.

options.text: Because real access patterns are skewed: a small set of popular keys receives most requests
options.explanation: Correct. Many cache-friendly workloads exhibit skew, but it must be measured, and requests repeat over time (temporal locality). If the cache holds the hottest 10% of keys, those may account for 80–95% of lookups.

questions.workedExample:
1. Hit ratio depends on **which keys are asked for**, not how many keys exist.
2. Suppose 1 million products, and the top 100,000 (10%) receive 90% of page views, as an explicit hypothetical distribution, not a universal e-commerce measurement.
3. If the cache holds those 100,000 products, then 90% of lookups find their key: the hit ratio is about 0.9 (90%).
4. The remaining 900,000 products share the other 10% of traffic, so caching them adds little.
5. So skew (popularity) plus repetition (temporal locality) is what makes small caches effective.

questions.prompt: Assume short-lived staleness is acceptable for displayed product prices, FX quotes and anonymous pages; payment authorization still requires authoritative transactional checks. Which of these workloads are **good** candidates for adding a cache? Select all that apply.

options.text: A product page read 50,000 times for every price update
options.explanation: Correct. A huge read-to-write ratio on the same key means each cached copy serves many reads before it needs refreshing.

options.text: A nightly job that scans every row of a 2 TB table exactly once
options.explanation: Not a good fit. Each row is read once, so there is no reuse. Caching it would just churn memory and evict useful data (this is called cache pollution).

options.text: A slow third-party exchange-rate API whose values change every few minutes
options.explanation: Correct. The call is expensive and slow, many requests share the same answer, and a staleness of a minute or so is acceptable. A short TTL fits well.

options.text: The account balance check that authorises a card payment
options.explanation: Not a good fit. Authorisation needs the latest committed balance. A stale cached value could approve a payment that overdraws the account.

options.text: A rendered homepage that is identical for all anonymous visitors
options.explanation: Correct. One copy serves everyone, it is expensive to render, and it can be cached at the reverse proxy or CDN for seconds to minutes.

questions.workedExample:
Check each workload against four tests:

1. **Read-heavy?** 2. **Repeated keys?** 3. **Staleness acceptable?** 4. **Expensive to produce?**

| Workload | Reuse | Stale OK | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| Product page | Very high | Seconds | Cache |
| Full table scan | None | n/a | Don't |
| FX rate API | High | Minutes | Cache |
| Balance for auth | High | No | Don't |
| Anonymous homepage | Very high | Seconds | Cache |

The scan fails on reuse; the balance check fails on staleness.

questions.prompt: A team stores shopping baskets *only* in Redis, with no persistence and no copy in the database, because "it is just a cache and it's fast". A Redis node is restarted during a deploy. What is the core design mistake?

options.text: They should have used Memcached, which keeps data across restarts
options.explanation: Memcached is an in-memory cache too: its optional warm restart only survives supported graceful restarts, not crashes, and it is not a durable home for data. Swapping products doesn't fix the fact that the data has no durable home.

options.text: Redis was being used as the system of record, so losing the cache lost data instead of just making things slower
options.explanation: Correct. Cached data must be disposable. Baskets that exist nowhere else are not a cache entry; they are primary data that needs a durable store (or Redis configured and operated as a database).

options.text: The TTL on the baskets was too long
options.explanation: TTL controls staleness, not durability. Any TTL would still lose the baskets on restart.

options.text: The hit ratio was too low
options.explanation: Hit ratio is irrelevant here. The problem is that there was nothing to fall back to on a miss.

questions.workedExample:
1. Apply the lesson's test: *if the cache is wiped, does the system get slower or wrong?*
2. Here, a wipe means customers' baskets vanish. That is **wrong**, not slower.
3. So Redis was acting as a database without a database's durability guarantees.
4. Fixes: write baskets to a durable store and cache them in front, or deliberately run Redis as a primary store (persistence, replication, backups) and treat it with database-level care.

lessons.title: Place response caches near the reader
lessons.summary: Compare browser, CDN and reverse-proxy caches, including privacy and fingerprinted asset names.
lessons.body:
Response caches save a trip to the origin or application. Their location determines who shares a copy and how easily you can replace it.

## The layers where caches live

A single web request can pass through half a dozen caches before it reaches the disk.

```
 Browser cache     (per user, HTTP headers)
      |
 CDN edge          (shared, near the user)
      |
 Reverse proxy     (Varnish / Nginx)
      |
 App server        (in-process memory)
      |
 Distributed cache (Redis / Memcached)
      |
 Database          (buffer pool, page cache)
      |
 Disk
```

Each layer sits closer to the user than the one below it. Caching closer to the user saves more latency but gives you less control over invalidation.

| Layer | Main saving | Who controls it |
|---|---|---|
| Browser | Network request | Browser and response policy |
| CDN edge | Origin trip | Provider configuration |
| Reverse proxy | Application work | Service operator |
| In-process | Network and decoding work | Application |
| Redis / Memcached | Database work | Cache operator |
| DB buffer pool | Storage reads | Database |

### Browser cache

The browser stores responses keyed by URL and obeys `Cache-Control`, `ETag` and friends. It is local to a browser profile, not necessarily one application account. A long freshness lifetime permits reuse; it does not guarantee retention. Supporting browsers can honour a `Clear-Site-Data` header on a later response, but there is no universal, immediate way to remotely empty every browser's cache. That is why static assets use **fingerprinted file names** such as `app.3f9a1c.js`. A new version is a new URL, so the old cached copy simply stops being requested.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: notices pinned around town
> A club pins a timetable on its own door, in the library and on dozens of noticeboards. Changing the copy on its own door is easy; tracking down every other copy is not. So instead the club prints next season's timetable under a new title and updates the one index board everyone checks first.
>
> **How it maps:** The noticeboards are caches at different distances from the origin. The further out a copy sits (CDN, then browsers), the less direct control you have over removing it. The new title is the fingerprinted URL, and the index board is the HTML page, which is revalidated and points at the new asset.
>
> **Where it stops:** Old notices stay up until someone removes them, whereas cached responses also expire or get evicted on their own. And unlike a public noticeboard, a shared cache must never show one person's private page to someone else.

### CDN edge

Large CDNs can keep copies in hundreds of points of presence (PoPs) worldwide, allowing an Australian user to fetch from a nearby edge rather than a distant origin. Actual placement and routing depend on the provider and request. It is a **shared** cache, so it must never store one user's private response and hand it to another. CDNs are covered in the networking module; here, remember that they are just another HTTP cache with a purge API.

### Reverse proxy

Varnish, Nginx (`proxy_cache`) or a cloud load balancer can cache full HTTP responses in front of your app servers. This is very effective for pages that are the same for every anonymous visitor, such as a news homepage.

## Key takeaways
- Browser caches retain copies per browser profile; fingerprinted URLs select a new asset version without a universal browser purge.
- CDNs and reverse proxies share responses, so private user data needs an explicit caching policy.
- Moving a cache towards the reader saves more downstream work while making invalidation less direct.

## Further reading
- [RFC 9111: HTTP Caching](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9111)
- [Caching overview — AWS](https://aws.amazon.com/caching/)
- [Historical latency estimates — not deployment measurements](https://gist.github.com/jboner/2841832)

questions.prompt: Why do sites serve JavaScript bundles with fingerprinted names like `app.3f9a1c.js` and a one-year cache lifetime?

options.text: Because browsers refuse to cache files without a hash in the name
options.explanation: Browsers cache any response permitted by its headers; the file name does not matter to the browser.

options.text: Changing content produces a new URL, so updated HTML requests the new asset without waiting for old cached entries to expire.
options.explanation: Correct. Fingerprinting avoids dependence on remotely clearing every browser. Long freshness does not guarantee cache retention or a perfect hit ratio.

options.text: Because the hash encrypts the file so CDNs cannot read it
options.explanation: The hash is a content fingerprint in the URL, not encryption. The CDN reads and serves the file normally.

options.text: Because it makes the file smaller
options.explanation: Adding a hash to the name has no effect on file size.

questions.workedExample:
1. A browser may reuse a fresh response without contacting the site.
2. Content-hashed asset URLs change when their bytes change.
3. Updated HTML refers to the new URL, which can be fetched independently of the old cached asset.
4. Clear-Site-Data can request cache clearing in supporting browsers once a response reaches them, but it is not a universal instant remote purge.
5. Eviction, user settings and stale HTML still affect cache hits and update visibility.

lessons.title: Compare local caches, shared caches and buffer pools
lessons.summary: Choose between per-process and remote application caches, and check database memory before adding a new service.
lessons.body:
Application caches store values your code chooses; database buffer pools store recently used pages. Both can avoid backend work, but they have different sharing and consistency costs.

### Application cache

This is the cache you code against. There are two flavours:

- **In-process** (a dictionary, Caffeine in Java, `functools.lru_cache` in Python). Avoids a network hop and can avoid serialisation; actual lookup cost depends on the implementation. But each server has its own copy, so 50 servers means 50 copies that can disagree, and memory is limited to one process.
- **Remote / distributed** (Redis, Memcached). A shared service (possibly with multiple replicas), accessed over the network at deployment-dependent latency. Survives app deploys and scales independently.

Many systems use both: a tiny in-process cache with a short TTL (say 1–5 seconds) in front of Redis, to absorb very hot keys.

### Database buffer pool

Databases cache too. PostgreSQL keeps recently used pages, normally 8 KiB (8,192 bytes) in `shared_buffers` and also relies on the operating system's page cache. PostgreSQL's docs suggest starting `shared_buffers` at about 25% of RAM on a dedicated server with at least 1 GB of RAM. MySQL's InnoDB has the **buffer pool**, which on a dedicated host is often given up to about 80% of RAM. Cached pages avoid storage reads, but the speedup depends on query execution, hardware and the rest of the workload.

> [!tip] The "free" cache
> Before adding Redis, check that your database's working set fits in RAM. Sizing the buffer pool correctly is often the cheapest caching win available.

## Key takeaways
- A local cache avoids network and decoding work but gives every process its own potentially stale copy.
- Redis or Memcached shares cached values across application servers and scales separately from them.
- Size and measure the database buffer pool before assuming an additional cache is the cheapest improvement.

## Further reading
- [PostgreSQL resource consumption (shared_buffers)](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-resource.html)
- [InnoDB buffer pool — MySQL](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/innodb-buffer-pool.html)
- [Caching overview — AWS](https://aws.amazon.com/caching/)

questions.prompt: You run 40 app servers, each with an in-process cache of user profiles (TTL 10 minutes). Assume no stale in-flight refill or replica lag, and no invalidation on writes. A user changes their display name. What will they most likely experience?

options.text: The name flips between old and new on refresh, depending on which server the load balancer picks, for up to 10 minutes
options.explanation: Correct. Each server has its own copy. Servers that cached the old name keep serving it until their entry expires, so requests landing on different servers see different values.

options.text: The new name appears everywhere immediately, because the database was updated
options.explanation: The database is updated, but 40 independent in-process caches still hold the old value until their TTL expires or they are explicitly invalidated.

options.text: The old name appears for exactly 10 minutes on every server, then changes everywhere at once
options.explanation: Each server cached the profile at a different time, so each entry expires at a different moment. There is no single synchronised switch-over.

options.text: The update fails, because in-process caches lock the row
options.explanation: In-process caches hold copies; they do not take database locks. The write succeeds.

questions.workedExample:
1. In-process means **one cache per server**: 40 separate copies.
2. Server A cached the profile at 10:00, server B at 10:07, server C never cached it.
3. The user renames at 10:08.
4. A request to C misses and reads the new name. A request to A shows the old name until 10:10. B shows it until 10:17.
5. The load balancer spreads requests, so the user sees the name flicker.

Fixes: use a shared cache with reliable invalidation (Redis alone does not ensure freshness), shorten the in-process TTL to a few seconds, or broadcast invalidations (for example via Redis pub/sub).

questions.prompt: You are choosing between an in-process cache and a shared Redis cache for product data on 30 app servers. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: An in-process lookup avoids a network round trip and can reduce latency.
options.explanation: Correct. The actual cost depends on language, data structure, serialization and workload; there is no universal 100 ns application lookup guarantee.

options.text: With one coalesced cold fill per server, up to 30 independent servers may load the same key.
options.explanation: Correct under that assumption. Without per-process coalescing, concurrent misses can produce more than one load per server.

options.text: A Redis cache is lost whenever an app server is redeployed
options.explanation: Incorrect. Redis runs as a separate service, so it survives app deploys. It is the in-process cache that is emptied on every restart.

options.text: An in-process cache keeps all 30 servers consistent with each other automatically
options.explanation: Incorrect. Each server holds an independent copy, so they can disagree until each entry expires or is invalidated.

options.text: A small in-process cache with a 1–5 s TTL in front of Redis can absorb very hot keys
options.explanation: Correct when short local staleness is acceptable. Local TTL bounds time since insertion, not total age inherited from Redis or a lagging source.

questions.workedExample:
1. Local caches avoid the network but each process has its own contents.
2. Shared Redis centralizes access, but replicas, invalidation races and stale origin data still affect consistency with the database.
3. A separate Redis service survives app restarts; a process-local cache does not.
4. Combining tiers can reduce hot-key load; measure latency and include every layer when setting freshness objectives.

lessons.title: Relate hit ratio to latency and database load
lessons.summary: See why every read pays the cache lookup, and why the miss ratio decides how much traffic still reaches the database.
lessons.body:
Measure both the time saved per request and the reads that still reach the database. A small latency improvement can hide a much larger change in backend load.

## Hit ratio and miss ratio

The **hit ratio** is the share of lookups the cache answers itself: 900 hits out of 1,000 lookups is a hit ratio of 0.9, or 90%. The **miss ratio** is everything else, here 10%. Count only lookups (reads), not writes, and count over a stated window such as a minute.

## Average read time

In the usual look-aside design every read checks the cache first, so **every** read pays the cache lookup, hit or miss. Only the misses then go on to pay for the backend as well. That gives the one relationship worth keeping in view:

```formula essential
T_avg = T_cache + (1 − h) × T_backend
where
T_avg: the average time to answer one read, in milliseconds (ms)
T_cache: the time for one cache lookup, hit or miss, in ms; measure it for your deployment
h: the hit ratio, between 0 and 1
(1 − h): the miss ratio, the fraction of reads that also go to the backend
T_backend: the time for the backend (for example the database) to answer one read, in ms
ms: milliseconds; 1 ms = 0.001 seconds
In words: everyone pays for the cache lookup; only the misses also pay for the database. The higher the hit ratio, the closer the average gets to the cache's own speed.
```

Two predictions follow directly:

- **A slower cache slows every read.** If the Redis round trip grows (say the cache moves to another availability zone), hits *and* misses both get slower, because both pay the lookup.
- **Past a high hit ratio, latency barely moves.** With a 1 ms cache in front of a 20 ms database, going from a 90% to a 99% hit ratio takes the average from about 3 ms to about 1.2 ms. Going on to 99.9% only reaches about 1.02 ms, because the cache lookup now dominates.

This simple model assumes a miss is a cache lookup followed by a backend read, one after the other. It ignores the small extra cost of writing the loaded value back, and it describes the *average* only. Slow outliers (tail latency) need percentiles, not this formula.

## Database load follows the miss ratio

The database sees only the misses. Its read rate is the total read rate multiplied by the miss ratio, so it is the miss ratio, not the hit ratio, that sizes your database.

| Hit ratio | Miss ratio | DB reads per 10,000 |
|---|---|---|
| 0% (cache checked) | 100% | 10,000 |
| 90% | 10% | 1,000 |
| 99% | 1% | 100 |
| 99.9% | 0.1% | 10 |

Notice the asymmetry. Between 90% and 99% the average read time falls by less than 2 ms, but **database load falls tenfold**. From 99% to 99.9% the latency chart hardly moves, yet backend load falls by another 10×. When hit ratios are high, think in miss ratios.

This is also why losing a cache is so dangerous. If the database is sized for a 1% miss ratio and the cache disappears, it suddenly receives 100× its usual traffic. The later avalanche and warming units cover this failure mode.

## Key takeaways
- Every read pays the cache lookup; only misses also pay the backend in this sequential model.
- Backend load is proportional to the miss ratio, which can change tenfold while mean latency barely moves.
- Averages omit tail latency, refill costs and overload effects; a database sized for the misses needs a plan for cache loss.

## Further reading
- [Caching best practices — AWS](https://aws.amazon.com/caching/best-practices/)
- [Caching overview — AWS](https://aws.amazon.com/caching/)

questions.prompt: Your service uses look-aside caching: every read checks Redis first and only misses go on to the database. The hit ratio is a steady 85%. After a network change, the Redis round trip rises from 1 ms to 3 ms; the database is unchanged. Which reads get slower?

options.text: Only the 15% of reads that miss, because hits never touch the network
options.explanation: A Redis hit still crosses the network to Redis. Only an in-process cache avoids that round trip; this design checks a remote cache on every read.

options.text: Every read, hits and misses alike, by about the extra 2 ms
options.explanation: Correct. In look-aside caching every read pays the cache lookup first, and misses pay it before going on to the database. A slower cache therefore adds its extra time to all reads, while the miss share stays the same.

options.text: No reads, because an 85% hit ratio hides cache latency
options.explanation: The hit ratio decides how many reads also pay the database, not whether reads pay the cache. Every read still waits for the lookup.

options.text: Only the 85% of reads that hit, because misses skip the cache once they are detected
options.explanation: A miss can only be detected by doing the lookup, so misses pay the slower round trip too before going on to the database.

questions.workedExample:
1. Ask what each kind of read waits for. A hit waits for the Redis lookup. A miss waits for the Redis lookup *and then* the database.
2. The network change made the Redis lookup 2 ms slower, so it adds about 2 ms to both kinds of read.
3. The database time and the 15% miss share are unchanged, so the misses' extra database cost is the same as before.
4. So the average read gets about 2 ms slower, and so does every individual read.
5. Design lesson: the cache's own latency is paid by 100% of reads. Measure it, keep the cache close to the application, and remember that a very fast backend can make a remote cache pointless for latency (the next unit's break-even idea).

questions.prompt: Your cache hit ratio rises from 99% to 99.9% after you double the cache size. Latency barely moves on the dashboard. What is the most important effect of this change?

options.text: Nothing significant: a 0.9 percentage point gain is noise
options.explanation: This judges the change by the hit ratio, but the backend experiences the miss ratio, which has fallen from 1% to 0.1%: a tenfold change.

options.text: Average latency falls by 10×
options.explanation: Once the hit ratio is high, the average is dominated by the cache lookup that every read pays. The few remaining database reads were already a small part of the average, so removing most of them changes it only slightly.

options.text: Database read load falls by roughly 10×
options.explanation: Correct. Misses fall from 1 in 100 reads to 1 in 1,000, so the database receives about a tenth of the reads it did. That frees capacity and reduces database queueing under load, even though the mean latency chart hardly moves.

options.text: The cache now needs less memory per key
options.explanation: Hit ratio has nothing to do with per-key memory. Doubling the cache used more memory in total.

questions.workedExample:
1. Separate the two effects of the change: what each read waits for, and what the database receives.
2. **Latency.** Every read still pays the cache lookup. At a 99% hit ratio the database part of the average was already small (1 read in 100), so cutting it further barely changes the mean. With a 1 ms cache and a 20 ms database, the mean moves from about 1.2 ms to about 1.02 ms.
3. **Database load.** The database receives only misses. 1 miss in 100 becomes 1 in 1,000, so database reads fall about tenfold.
4. Conclusion: once hit ratios are high, think in miss ratios. The miss ratio is what decides how big the database must be.

questions.prompt: Your database can sustain 5,000 reads/s. Peak traffic is 200,000 reads/s and the cache hit ratio is 98%. A bad deploy flushes the cache. Roughly what happens, and what does it tell you about capacity planning?

options.text: The database sees about 4,000 reads/s before and after, because the hit ratio is a property of the workload
options.explanation: Hit ratio depends on what the cache currently holds. An empty cache has a hit ratio near 0%, so almost every request goes to the database.

options.text: Load rises to 10,000/s, double the normal miss rate
options.explanation: This underestimates badly. A flushed cache does not merely double misses; it turns almost every request into a miss until it warms up.

options.text: Nothing changes for the database; the app servers just get slower
options.explanation: The app servers get slower because they are waiting on the database, which is now receiving almost all traffic.

options.text: The database load jumps from about 4,000/s to nearly 200,000/s, 40× its capacity, so it falls over unless traffic is shed or the cache refills quickly
options.explanation: Correct. Normally only about 2% of reads miss, roughly 4,000 a second, which fits within the 5,000/s capacity. With an empty cache almost every read misses, so the database is offered close to the full 200,000/s: dozens of times its capacity. The cache was carrying load the database was never sized for.

questions.workedExample:
1. The database sees the miss ratio times the total read rate.
2. Normally the miss ratio is 2%, so the database gets about 4,000 of the 200,000 reads a second: under its 5,000/s limit.
3. Right after the flush the cache is empty and the hit ratio is near zero, so the database is offered nearly all 200,000 reads a second, around 40 times what it can sustain.
4. Queries queue, latency soars and connections run out. The cache refills slowly because the database is too busy to answer the misses that would refill it.
5. Capacity-planning lesson: if the backend cannot survive the cache disappearing, the cache is **critical infrastructure**. Plan for it with replicas, warming, request coalescing, rate limits on misses and load shedding (covered in the later failure-mode units).

lessons.title: Judge stacked caches and when a cache pays off
lessons.summary: Follow misses through stacked caches and decide whether an extra lookup is worth its latency.
lessons.body:
An upper cache changes the traffic a lower one sees. Judge each layer by what it saves the layer below, then compare the extra lookup cost with the backend time it avoids.

## Stacked caches

When caches sit in layers, each one sees only the misses of the layer above. A read reaches the database only if it misses *every* layer, so the share of reads that gets through is the first layer's miss ratio multiplied by the second layer's miss ratio, and so on.

For example, an in-process cache that answers half of all reads, in front of a Redis cache that answers 90% of what reaches it, lets through half of a tenth: 5% of reads reach the database, a combined hit ratio of 95%. This only works if each layer's hit ratio is measured on the traffic that actually reaches it.

A consequence surprises people: adding a fast upper layer usually makes the second layer's **own** hit ratio look worse. The in-process cache takes the hottest keys, so Redis is left with the harder, less repetitive reads. That is not Redis getting worse. Judge each layer by what it saves the layer below, and judge the stack by the share of reads that still reach the database.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a sieve stack
> Gravel is shaken through a coarse sieve and then a fine one. The fine sieve now only sees what the coarse one let through, so it catches a smaller share of what reaches it than it would on its own, even though it works exactly as before. What matters is what ends up in the bin under the stack.
>
> **How it maps:** Each sieve is a cache layer, what passes through is the misses, and the second sieve's "catch rate" is the second cache's hit ratio measured on the traffic that reaches it. The bin under the stack is the database.
>
> **Where it stops:** Sieves sort by a fixed property (size). Caches decide by what they currently hold, which changes with eviction, expiry and the layer above.

## When does a cache lookup pay for itself?

A cache in front of a backend makes every read pay the lookup, and saves the backend time only on hits. If the backend is already fast or the hit ratio is low, the lookup can cost more than it saves. The hit ratio at which the two balance is the **break-even hit ratio**.

```formula reference
h_be = T_cache / T_backend
where
h_be: the break-even hit ratio, between 0 and 1; below it, the cache makes average latency worse than no cache
T_cache: the time for one cache lookup, in milliseconds (ms)
T_backend: the time for one backend read, in ms
ms: milliseconds; 1 ms = 0.001 seconds
In words: a cache only improves average latency once its hit ratio beats the ratio of cache time to backend time. A 1 ms cache in front of a 20 ms database breaks even at about a 5% hit ratio; in front of a 2 ms backend it needs about 50%.
```

So a remote cache in front of a slow query almost always helps latency, while the same cache in front of a fast, well-cached database may not. Latency is not the only reason to cache, though: even a low hit ratio removes some backend load, and that can matter more.

## Key takeaways
- The share of reads reaching the database is the product of the miss ratios each layer sees on its own incoming traffic.
- A second-tier cache can show a weaker hit ratio because the cache in front already absorbed the hottest keys.
- A lookup only improves average latency when the hit ratio beats cache time divided by backend time; backend-load savings are a separate benefit.

## Further reading
- [Caching overview — AWS](https://aws.amazon.com/caching/)
- [Cache (computing) — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cache_(computing))

questions.prompt: You add an in-process cache on each app server in front of Redis. It answers about 60% of reads. Afterwards Redis's own hit ratio falls from 90% to 80%, while the share of all reads reaching the database falls slightly. A teammate says "Redis got worse, let's give it more memory". What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Redis is evicting more keys since the change, so more memory is the fix
options.explanation: Nothing about the change added keys or reduced Redis's memory. The drop reflects a different mix of traffic reaching Redis, not new capacity pressure; check evictions before buying memory.

options.text: Redis now sees only what the in-process caches missed: the hottest keys are gone, so its remaining traffic is harder to hit. Judge the stack by the share of reads reaching the database, which improved
options.explanation: Correct. Each layer's hit ratio is measured on the traffic that reaches it. The upper layer skims off the most repetitive reads, so Redis's ratio drops even though it is working as before, and the database is better off.

options.text: Redis's hit ratio should include the reads the in-process cache answered, so it is really above 90%
options.explanation: Reads answered by the in-process cache never reached Redis, so they are not Redis hits. Mixing them in hides what each layer does and double-counts the upper layer's work.

options.text: Remove the in-process cache: a lower Redis hit ratio means more database load
options.explanation: The scenario says database load fell. The lower Redis ratio is measured on fewer, harder reads; it does not mean more misses reach the database.

questions.workedExample:
1. Follow 100 reads. The in-process caches answer about 60, so about 40 reach Redis.
2. Those 40 exclude the hottest keys, which the local caches now serve. What reaches Redis is less repetitive, so a smaller share of it hits: 80% instead of 90%.
3. Redis misses about 8 of its 40, so about 8 reads in 100 reach the database. Before the change, Redis alone missed about 10 in 100.
4. So the stack improved, even though one of its numbers looks worse.
5. Rule: a read reaches the database only if it misses every layer, so multiply the miss ratios each layer sees. Judge each layer by what it saves the layer below.

questions.prompt: A cache lookup only improves *average* read latency when the hit ratio is higher than the cache's lookup time divided by the backend's read time. In which situation is adding a remote cache **least** likely to improve average latency?

options.text: A 1 ms cache in front of a 50 ms reporting query, with a 30% hit ratio
options.explanation: The cache costs 1 ms but saves 50 ms on each hit, so even a small hit ratio more than repays it. Here the break-even is only about 2%.

options.text: A 1 ms cache in front of a 20 ms database, with a 95% hit ratio
options.explanation: Far above the break-even of about 5%: the average falls from 20 ms to roughly 2 ms.

options.text: A 1 ms cache in front of a 2 ms primary-key lookup, with a 30% hit ratio
options.explanation: Correct. The lookup costs half as much as the backend read, so the cache needs about a 50% hit ratio just to break even. At 30%, average latency gets worse, though the cache may still remove some backend load.

options.text: An in-process cache taking microseconds in front of a 20 ms remote API, with a 20% hit ratio
options.explanation: A lookup that costs almost nothing breaks even at an almost-zero hit ratio, so even 20% hits help.

questions.workedExample:
1. Compare what the lookup costs every read with what a hit saves.
2. Every read pays the cache time; only hits avoid the backend time. So the lookup pays off once the hit ratio beats cache time ÷ backend time.
3. Slow backend or near-free cache: the ratio is tiny, so almost any hit ratio helps (options A, B and D).
4. Fast backend with a remote cache (1 ms vs 2 ms): the ratio is one half. At a 30% hit ratio, the lookup adds more than the hits save.
5. Before rejecting the cache, check whether you wanted latency or backend-load relief: the 30% of reads it absorbs may still matter to a struggling database.

lessons.title: Size a cache from its measured working set
lessons.summary: Estimate payload memory from active keys, value size and measured overhead, then reserve deployment headroom.
lessons.body:
The number of registered records is usually less useful than the number of distinct keys read during the window you want to cover. Payload arithmetic is the starting point for sizing, not a complete machine recommendation.

## Sizing: how big should it be?

You rarely need to cache everything. Because access is skewed, the share of keys worth caching depends on the observed popularity distribution. The usual approach is:

1. Estimate the **working set**: the distinct keys touched in a typical window (an hour or a day). For a user-profile cache that is today's active users, not everyone who ever registered.
2. Multiply by the average size of one value plus the per-key overhead: the key itself, metadata and allocator waste. Measure that overhead with representative objects (Redis's `MEMORY USAGE` command reports a key's bytes); no fixed per-key overhead applies to every cache and data shape.
3. Add headroom for what the payload estimate leaves out: allocator fragmentation, client and replication buffers, snapshot copy-on-write and growth.
4. Measure the hit ratio at a few sizes. The curve of hit ratio against cache size flattens out; stop where extra memory stops buying meaningful hits.

```formula reference
M = K × (S_v + S_o)
where
M: the memory needed for the cached data, in bytes (B)
K: the number of distinct keys in the working set
S_v: the average size of one cached value, in bytes
S_o: the average overhead per key (the key itself, metadata and allocator waste), in bytes; measure it for your cache and data
B: bytes; 1 GB = 1,000,000,000 B
In words: payload memory is the number of active keys times what each one costs, value plus overhead. For example, 5 million active profiles of about 2 KB each, with about 100 bytes of measured overhead, need roughly 10.5 GB before any headroom.
```

The most common sizing mistakes are using all registered records instead of active ones (oversizing by the inactive majority), forgetting per-key overhead (which can rival the value for small items), and treating the payload total as the machine size.

## Key takeaways
- Estimate distinct active keys over a realistic window instead of caching every possible record.
- Include measured key, allocator and metadata overhead as well as the values themselves.
- Add measured fragmentation, buffers, replication and snapshot headroom, then compare hit ratios at different capacities.

## Further reading
- [MEMORY USAGE — Redis](https://redis.io/docs/latest/commands/memory-usage/)
- [Key eviction — Redis docs](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/reference/eviction/)

questions.prompt: You have 20 million registered users, of whom about 4 million are active on a typical day. Each cached session object is about 1.5 KB. A teammate proposes buying a Redis node sized as "20 million × 1.5 KB". Which sizing plan is soundest?

options.text: Start from the 4 million daily active keys, add per-key overhead measured on representative objects, add headroom for fragmentation, buffers and snapshots, then compare hit ratios at a few sizes
options.explanation: Correct. The working set is what is actually read in the window you want to cover. Overhead and headroom are real memory the payload estimate omits, and the hit-ratio curve tells you where extra memory stops paying.

options.text: Size for all 20 million registered users so that every possible session is cached
options.explanation: This pays for memory to hold sessions that are mostly not read today. Because access is skewed towards active users, those extra keys buy few hits.

options.text: 4 million × 1.5 KB exactly, since values are the only thing that uses memory
options.explanation: Keys, metadata and allocator waste also use memory, and for small values that overhead can be a large fraction. The node also needs headroom beyond the payload.

options.text: Cache 20% of registered users, because the 80/20 rule always holds
options.explanation: Skew is common, but a fixed 80/20 split is not universal. Measure the actual active set and hit-ratio curve rather than assuming a ratio.

questions.workedExample:
1. Ask which keys will actually be read in the window: about 4 million active users today, not 20 million registered.
2. Each key costs its value plus overhead. Measure the overhead (for example with Redis's `MEMORY USAGE`) instead of assuming a figure.
3. The values alone come to about 6 GB (4 million × 1.5 KB); measured overhead adds to that. This payload total is the starting point, not the machine size.
4. Add measured headroom for allocator fragmentation, client and replication buffers, and snapshot copy-on-write.
5. Finally test a few sizes: if the hit-ratio curve has flattened, a smaller cache may give almost the same hits.

lessons.title: Choose who loads a cache miss
lessons.summary: Compare application-managed cache-aside with read-through loaders and per-process miss coalescing.
lessons.body:
Once you have decided to cache, you have to decide **who loads the cache, and what happens on a write**. These choices are called caching strategies (or patterns). They differ in who is responsible for the cache, how fresh the data is, and what can be lost when something crashes.

Read strategies decide how data gets *into* the cache. Write strategies decide what happens when data *changes*. Real systems combine one of each.

## Cache-aside (lazy loading)

This is the most common pattern, and the default for Redis and Memcached. The application talks to both the cache and the database. The cache knows nothing about the database.

```
 read(key):
   1. GET key from cache ---- hit --> return
   2. miss: SELECT from DB
   3. SET key in cache (with TTL)
   4. return value
```

The following uses application-specific database and serialization adapters; it illustrates control flow rather than a complete library integration.

```python
def get_user(user_id):
    key = f"user:{user_id}"
    cached = redis.get(key)
    if cached is not None:
        # A hit skips both DB and refill.
        return deserialise(cached)
    # A miss reads the source of truth.
    user = db.query(
        "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id=%s",
        user_id)
    if user is not None:
        # Cache successful reads for 300 s.
        redis.set(key, serialise(user),
                  ex=300)
    return user
```

On a write, the application updates the database and then **deletes** the cache key, so the next read reloads it.

Why delete rather than overwrite with the new value? Deleting is idempotent and cheap, and it avoids two concurrent writers racing to `SET` their versions in the wrong order (the older value could land last and stick). The later invalidation units trace the races that remain.

**Strengths**

- Only data that is actually requested gets cached, so memory is not wasted.
- With timeouts, fallback and sufficient origin capacity, cache failure can fall back to the database; otherwise the miss surge can overload it.
- Works with any database and any cache.

**Weaknesses**

- The first read of each key is a miss, which costs three trips (cache, DB, cache).
- Cache logic is spread through application code.
- There is a window where the cache and database disagree, and some interleavings of concurrent reads and writes can leave stale data in the cache for a whole TTL (the later invalidation units).

## Read-through

The cache sits **in line**: the app only talks to the cache, and on a miss the cache itself loads from the database using a loader you configure.

```
 App --> Cache --miss--> DB
     <--       <--------
```

The data flow is the same as cache-aside; the difference is **where the code lives**. Examples include Caffeine's `LoadingCache` in Java, NCache, and DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX), which is a read-through and write-through cache in front of DynamoDB.

Read-through keeps application code simple, and a good library will **coalesce** concurrent misses for the same key into one database query. Note that an in-process library coalesces per process: with 20 app servers, a cold key can still cause up to 20 queries. The cost is coupling: the cache must know how to talk to your database.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: the shop counter and the stockroom
> In one shop, staff check the shelf and, if it is empty, walk to the stockroom themselves and restock the shelf on the way back. In another, staff only ever ask the counter assistant, who fetches from the stockroom when the shelf is empty.
>
> **How it maps:** The shelf is the cache and the stockroom is the database. Staff fetching for themselves is cache-aside: the application holds the loading logic. The counter assistant is read-through: the cache layer owns the loader, so every caller gets the same restocking rules, and one trip can serve everyone queuing for the same item (coalescing).
>
> **Where it stops:** Shelves hold the real goods; a cache holds copies that can go stale when the database changes. And one assistant per shop is like coalescing per process: several shops (servers) can still send several people to the stockroom for the same item.

## Key takeaways
- Cache-aside keeps the database loader in application code; read-through puts it in the cache or library.
- Load only requested keys and invalidate after database writes, while retaining a TTL and safe fallback capacity.
- A read-through library can combine concurrent misses inside one process; multiple servers can still issue multiple loads.

## Further reading
- [Cache-aside pattern — Azure Architecture Center](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/cache-aside)
- [Caching strategies — Amazon ElastiCache docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonElastiCache/latest/dg/Strategies.html)

questions.prompt: In the **cache-aside** pattern, who is responsible for loading data into the cache on a miss?

options.text: The cache, using a loader function configured for the database
options.explanation: That describes read-through. In cache-aside the cache is a passive key-value store that knows nothing about the database.

options.text: The database, which pushes changes into the cache
options.explanation: Pushing changes from the database (for example via change data capture) is an invalidation technique, not the definition of cache-aside.

options.text: The application: it checks the cache, reads the database on a miss, then writes the value to the cache
options.explanation: Correct. The application sits "aside" both stores and orchestrates them. This is the default pattern with Redis and Memcached.

options.text: Nobody: cache-aside only caches values that were written
options.explanation: Caching values on write is write-through. Cache-aside is lazy: it caches on read misses.

questions.workedExample:
1. Request for `user:42` arrives at the app.
2. App calls `GET user:42` on Redis and gets nothing (miss).
3. App queries the database itself.
4. App calls `SET user:42 <value> EX 300`.
5. App returns the value.

Every step is in application code, so the app owns the cache logic. In read-through, steps 3–4 would happen inside the cache library instead.

questions.prompt: Under a sudden spike, within one process, 500 requests for the same uncached key arrive within 10 ms. Which approach prevents 500 identical database queries with the least application code?

options.text: Plain cache-aside with a longer TTL
options.explanation: A longer TTL does not help the first load: all 500 requests miss before anyone has populated the key, so all 500 query the database.

options.text: Write-around
options.explanation: Write-around affects writes. This scenario is entirely about concurrent reads.

options.text: A read-through cache library that coalesces concurrent loads for the same key
options.explanation: Correct. Libraries such as Caffeine's `LoadingCache` run the loader once per key and make the other callers wait for the same result, so 500 misses become 1 query.

options.text: Write-back with a 1 s flush interval
options.explanation: Write-back changes when writes reach the database; it does nothing to stop concurrent read misses.

questions.workedExample:
1. With naive cache-aside, each of the 500 requests runs `GET` (miss) → `SELECT` → `SET` independently, giving 500 queries.
2. A coalescing read-through cache keeps a map of in-flight loads per key.
3. Request 1 starts the load. Requests 2–500 find a pending load and wait for its result.
4. Result: 1 query, 500 responses.
5. You can build the same thing by hand in cache-aside (Go's `singleflight`, or a short Redis lock), as the later stampede and coalescing unit shows, but read-through libraries often give it to you for free.
6. One caveat: in-process coalescing is per server. With 20 app servers, the 500 requests become at most 20 queries, which is usually fine.

questions.prompt: An app uses cache-aside: on a read miss it queries the database and sets the key with a TTL. The application developers find the miss path repeated in 40 places and keep forgetting to add the TTL. Which change addresses this most directly?

options.text: Switch to write-back so the cache handles writes
options.explanation: Write-back changes the write path. The duplication here is in the read-miss logic.

options.text: Remove the TTL everywhere for consistency
options.explanation: Removing TTLs removes the safety net that repairs stale or orphaned entries. Consistency of code is not worth that.

options.text: Move to a read-through layer: one loader function per entity type, so the cache owns loading and applies the TTL in one place
options.explanation: Correct. Read-through moves the miss-handling into the cache layer, so it is written once, the TTL is configured once, and concurrent misses can be coalesced.

options.text: Cache everything at application start-up so there are no misses
options.explanation: Pre-loading everything wastes memory on unread data and still needs a miss path for new or evicted keys.

questions.workedExample:
1. Cache-aside puts `GET → miss → SELECT → SET` in **application code**, wherever data is read.
2. 40 copies means 40 chances to forget the TTL or serialise differently.
3. Read-through has the same data flow but the code lives in the cache layer:

Illustrative adapter API (not a complete library program):

```python
# Configure one shared miss path.
cache = LoadingCache(
    loader=load_user, ttl=300)
# A miss invokes the configured loader.
user = cache.get(user_id)
```

4. Now the TTL is set in one place, and a good library also coalesces concurrent misses.
5. The trade-off is coupling: the cache layer now has to know how to load each entity.

lessons.title: Choose write-through or write-around
lessons.summary: Handle partial failures in synchronous cache writes and avoid filling a cache with write-only records.
lessons.body:
A write policy decides which stores receive an update before it is acknowledged. It must also handle ordering, failures and the cached copy that was already present.

## Write-through

On every write, the data is written to the cache **and** to the database synchronously, before the write is acknowledged.

```
 write(key, v):
   App --> Cache --> DB
   ack only after both succeed
```

**Strengths**

- Acknowledging both writes can make read-after-write fresh when ordering and failure handling are correct. Two independent writes alone do not prevent concurrent writers leaving a stale cache value.
- Nothing is lost if the cache crashes, because the database already has it.

**Weaknesses**

- The acknowledgement waits for the required writes; total latency depends on their ordering and possible overlap.
- Data that is written but never read still fills the cache (often fixed by pairing with a TTL).
- If the DB write succeeds and the cache write fails (or the reverse), you need a rule for which one wins. In practice, write to the DB first and treat the cache as best-effort.

## Write-around

Writes go **straight to the database**, bypassing the cache. The cache is only filled on reads (usually by cache-aside), and any existing cached copy is invalidated.

This suits data that is written once and rarely read soon afterwards, such as logs, audit records, or uploads. It avoids filling the cache with data nobody asks for. The cost is that a read straight after a write is a miss.

Strictly, "update the DB then delete the key" in cache-aside is write-around plus invalidation, and that is the most common combination in practice.

## Comparing them

The table includes write-back, which the next unit covers in detail: it acknowledges a write once the cache has it and updates the database later.

| Strategy | Write latency | Fresh after write | Risk |
|---|---|---|---|
| Write-through | High (2 writes) | With ordering | Concurrent writes / failures |
| Write-back | Very low | Cache yes, DB no | Data loss on crash |
| Write-around | DB only | Miss on next read | Read-after-write miss |

| Read strategy | Code lives in | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Cache-aside | Application | Simple, resilient, most common |
| Read-through | Cache / library | Cleaner code, can coalesce misses |

## Choosing in practice

1. **Default to cache-aside with delete-on-write and a TTL.** It is a practical default when staleness is acceptable. TTL bounds entry residence rather than source-data age; failures still require safe fallback, origin capacity and reliable refill.
2. Use **read-through** when a library gives it to you cheaply (Caffeine, DAX) and you want built-in miss coalescing.
3. Add **write-through** when reads straight after writes are common and must hit, such as a user editing then viewing their profile.
4. Use **write-back** only for high-volume, loss-tolerant writes, or when the cache layer is designed to be durable.
5. Use **write-around** for write-heavy, read-rarely data.

## Key takeaways
- Write-through waits for required database and cache writes; concurrency and partial failures still need a policy.
- Write-around stores writes in the database, invalidates an existing copy and fills the cache on a later read.
- Avoid populating a cache with millions of writes that almost nobody reads; choose policies from the access pattern.

## Further reading
- [Cache-aside pattern — Azure Architecture Center](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/cache-aside)
- [Caching best practices — AWS](https://aws.amazon.com/caching/best-practices/)
- [System Design Primer — caching section](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer)

questions.prompt: Which strategy writes data **only to the database**, leaving the cache to be filled later by reads?

options.text: Write-through
options.explanation: Write-through writes to both cache and database synchronously.

options.text: Write-back
options.explanation: Write-back writes to the cache first and the database later; it is the opposite of bypassing the cache.

options.text: Read-through
options.explanation: Read-through is a read strategy describing who loads data on a miss, not a write strategy.

options.text: Write-around
options.explanation: Correct. Writes go around the cache straight to the database. It suits data that is written often but read rarely, at the cost of a miss on the first read after a write.

questions.workedExample:
1. Ask: on a write, where does data go?
2. Write-through: cache + DB. Write-back: cache, then DB later. Write-around: DB only.
3. Read-through does not describe writes at all.
4. So the answer is write-around. A typical use is log or audit data, which is written constantly and rarely read straight away.

questions.prompt: Users complain that after editing their profile, the profile page still shows the old data for a few seconds. The app uses cache-aside, updating the DB then letting the 60 s TTL expire. Which change most directly fixes this?

options.text: Increase the TTL to 10 minutes
options.explanation: A longer TTL makes the stale window longer, not shorter.

options.text: Delete (or overwrite) the cache key immediately after the database update commits
options.explanation: Correct for the simple sequential path: invalidate after commit rather than waiting for expiry. Concurrent stale fills, reordered cache writes and failures still require leases/versioning or an authoritative read path when strict freshness matters.

options.text: Switch to write-around without invalidation
options.explanation: Write-around without invalidation is what the app is effectively doing now: the DB is updated, but the stale cached copy remains until TTL.

options.text: Move the cache into each app server's process
options.explanation: In-process caching adds more copies and makes staleness worse, since each server must be invalidated separately.

questions.workedExample:
1. Current flow: `UPDATE users ...` and nothing else. The cache still holds the old profile until its TTL (up to 60 s) runs out.
2. Fix: after the commit, `DEL user:42`.
3. The next read misses, loads the new row and caches it.
4. In the sequential successful path the stale window ends at deletion; there is no unconditional millisecond bound under races or failures.
5. Keep the TTL anyway: if a delete is ever lost (network blip), expiry still repairs the cache eventually.

questions.prompt: With write-through, the app writes to Redis, then to Postgres. Redis succeeds but the Postgres transaction fails on a constraint violation. What state are you in, and what is the usual fix?

options.text: The cache now holds a value that never existed in the database; write to the DB first and only then update or delete the cache
options.explanation: Correct. Readers would see data that was rejected. Ordering the DB write first means a failed write leaves the cache untouched, and a cache failure after commit leaves only a stale entry, which deletion or a TTL repairs.

options.text: Consistent: Postgres rolled back, so Redis automatically rolls back too
options.explanation: Redis and Postgres do not share a transaction. A Postgres rollback does nothing to a value already set in Redis.

options.text: Postgres will retry until it succeeds, so the states will converge
options.explanation: A constraint violation is a permanent rejection, not a transient error. Retrying fails the same way.

options.text: This cannot happen with write-through, because write-through uses two-phase commit
options.explanation: Write-through is a pattern, not a protocol. Common implementations do not use two-phase commit between the cache and database.

questions.workedExample:
1. Sequence: `SET user:42 {...new...}` succeeds, then `UPDATE users ...` fails (for example a unique email clash).
2. Postgres still holds the old row; Redis holds a version that was never committed.
3. Readers hitting Redis see phantom data until a TTL or the next write.
4. Fix the order: commit to the DB first (it is the source of truth and can reject writes), then update or delete the cache.
5. If the cache step fails after a successful commit, you have a *stale* entry, not a *phantom* one, and a delete-retry or TTL repairs it.

questions.prompt: Two requests update the same product price at almost the same moment. Each one writes the database and then **overwrites** the cache with its own new value using `SET`. Writer A commits £10, then writer B commits £12, but A's `SET` reaches Redis after B's. What is the result?

options.text: Redis holds £12, matching the database, because the last database commit always wins in the cache
options.explanation: The cache has no idea about commit order. Whichever `SET` arrives last wins in Redis, and here that is A's.

options.text: Redis holds £10 while the database holds £12, and it stays wrong until the TTL expires or the next write
options.explanation: Correct. Overwriting on write lets slow network paths reorder updates. Deleting the key instead means both writers do the same idempotent thing, and the next read loads £12.

options.text: Redis rejects A's `SET` because it is older
options.explanation: Plain `SET` has no versioning. It accepts whatever arrives last.

options.text: Both writes fail with a conflict error
options.explanation: Neither the database nor Redis detects a conflict here. Both writes succeed, which is exactly why the cache ends up wrong.

questions.workedExample:
1. Database order: A (£10) then B (£12). Database = **£12**.
2. Cache order: B's `SET £12`, then A's delayed `SET £10`. Cache = **£10**.
3. Readers now get £10 until the TTL expires.
4. With delete-on-write:

```
A: commit £10, DEL price:9
B: commit £12, DEL price:9
```

The order of deletes no longer matters; the next read misses and loads £12.

Delete-on-write closes this particular race. The later stale-refill unit covers the read/write race it does not close.

questions.prompt: Your product catalogue uses write-through caching with a 24-hour TTL. A nightly job re-imports 10 million product rows, of which only about 50,000 are viewed on a typical day. The morning after each import, the cache hit ratio collapses. What is the best change?

options.text: Make the import use write-around: write to the database and delete any cached copy, so only products that are actually read get cached
options.explanation: Correct. Write-through on a bulk import caches 10 million mostly-unread rows, which evicts the hot 50,000. Bypassing population avoids filling the cache with cold imported rows. Invalidating changed hot rows still causes their next reads to miss.

options.text: Increase the TTL to 7 days so imported entries last longer
options.explanation: The problem is that unread entries are flooding the cache and evicting hot ones. Keeping them longer makes it worse.

options.text: Switch the import to write-back so it finishes faster
options.explanation: Write-back still puts all 10 million rows in the cache, and adds a risk of data loss to a bulk import.

options.text: Double the cache size so all 10 million rows fit
options.explanation: This might work, but it buys a lot of memory to store data that is almost never read. Changing the write path is far cheaper.

questions.workedExample:
1. Write-through puts every written row into the cache: 10 million entries.
2. Only ~50,000 (0.5%) are read on a typical day.
3. The cache has a fixed size, so the imported rows evict the hot entries (cache pollution).
4. In the morning, readers miss on the hot products until they reload: the hit ratio collapses.
5. Write-around for the import (write DB, `DEL` the key) keeps the cache holding only what readers asked for.

Rule of thumb: write-through suits writes that are likely to be read soon; bulk or write-heavy paths should go around the cache.

lessons.title: Bound the loss window of write-back caching
lessons.summary: Calculate unflushed acknowledged writes and handle durable baselines, batching and flush ordering.
lessons.body:
Write-back acknowledges a cache write before the database has it. That lowers latency and combines updates, but temporarily makes the cache authoritative for the unflushed changes.

## Write-back (write-behind)

Writes go to the cache only, and are acknowledged immediately. The cache flushes them to the database **later**, asynchronously, often in batches.

```
 write --> Cache (ack)
             |  later, batched
             v
             DB
```

Many CPU caches, the operating system page cache and database buffer pools use write-back: dirty data is written to the next memory or storage level later. A database can first make a transaction durable in its write-ahead log, so delayed buffer-page writes do not imply the same loss window as an unlogged application cache.

**Strengths**

- Very low write latency.
- Absorbs bursts and **coalesces** repeated writes. A counter incremented 1,000 times a second can be flushed once a second as a single write.

**Weaknesses**

- **Data loss.** If the cache node dies before flushing, the acknowledged writes are gone, unless the cache itself is durable (replicated, with a write-ahead log).
- The database is behind the cache, so anything reading the database directly (reports, other services) sees old data.
- Ordering and failure handling of the flush are hard to get right.

How much can a crash lose? Everything acknowledged since the last *successful* flush. With steady writes and on-time flushes, that is about one flush interval's worth of writes: the counter above, flushed every second, risks about a second of increments; flushed every 5 s, about five seconds' worth. Longer intervals coalesce more writes but widen the loss window. A late or failed flush makes the real window longer than the planned interval, so measure the time since the last successful flush rather than trusting the schedule.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: the waiter's order pad
> A busy waiter jots orders on a pad, tells each table "got it", and takes the pad to the kitchen every few minutes rather than walking back after every order.
>
> **How it maps:** The pad is the write-back cache, "got it" is the acknowledgement, and the trip to the kitchen is the batched flush to the database. Fewer trips means less walking (fewer database writes), and repeated changes to one table's order collapse into one line (coalescing).
>
> **Where it stops:** If the waiter loses the pad, the customers were already told "got it" and those orders are simply gone, which is the write-back loss window. Unlike a waiter, the cache cannot ask customers to repeat themselves, and the kitchen (database) cannot see anything still on the pad.

> [!warning] Write-back changes your source of truth
> With write-back, the cache temporarily *is* the source of truth for recent writes. You need the durability guarantees of a database from it. Use it only where its measured loss window (including delayed or failed flushes) is tolerable (view counters, analytics) or where the cache is genuinely durable.

> [!example] A social feed counter
> Likes on a viral post may arrive at 20,000 per second. A single PostgreSQL row may become a contention bottleneck; benchmark the actual transaction path. Instead, `INCR post:123:likes` in Redis (write-back) and flush the total to Postgres every few seconds. Whether any lost likes are acceptable is a product decision. Restore the baseline from durable state after cache loss and handle flush ordering/idempotency; blindly persisting a reset or old total can lose previously saved counts.

## Key takeaways
- Acknowledged changes are vulnerable until a successful flush unless the cache has adequate durability.
- The loss estimate uses the actual time since the last successful flush; delays and failures enlarge it.
- Restore durable counter baselines after cache loss and make flush ordering and retries safe.

## Further reading
- [Cache writing policies — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cache_(computing))
- [Redis persistence](https://redis.io/docs/latest/operate/oss_and_stack/management/persistence/)

questions.prompt: A service uses **write-back** caching for shopping-basket updates. A cache node crashes 3 seconds after acknowledging a customer's "add to basket". The next flush is due 5 seconds after that acknowledgement; the cache has neither persistence nor replication. What happens?

options.text: The item is lost: it was acknowledged but never flushed to the database
options.explanation: Correct. The write lived only in the crashed node's memory. This is the core risk of write-back without a durable, replicated cache.

options.text: The item is safe, because write-back writes to the database first
options.explanation: That is the opposite of write-back. Write-back acknowledges after writing to the cache only and writes the database later.

options.text: The item is delayed until the node restarts, then flushed
options.explanation: An in-memory cache without persistence loses its contents on a crash. There is nothing left to flush after a restart.

options.text: The database rejects later writes until it is reconciled with the cache
options.explanation: The database knows nothing about the pending writes, so there is nothing for it to reconcile against.

questions.workedExample:
Timeline:

```
0 s  write to cache, ACK to user
3 s  cache node crashes
5 s  flush would have happened
```

1. At 0 s the only copy of the change is in cache RAM.
2. The crash at 3 s destroys it.
3. The database never received it, so the basket is missing the item.

To use write-back safely you need a failure-tested durability protocol in the cache; asynchronous replication alone can lose acknowledged writes, or a workload where losing up to one flush interval of writes is acceptable.

questions.prompt: You are choosing a strategy for a **page-view counter** incremented 30,000 times per second on a popular article. Losing a few seconds of counts in a crash is acceptable. Assume each scheduled flush succeeds on time. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: Write-back lets you coalesce thousands of increments into one database write per flush
options.explanation: Correct. `INCR` in Redis absorbs each increment, and a flush every second writes the accumulated count once, so the database sees one write per flush instead of 30,000 contended row updates.

options.text: Write-through would still send 30,000 writes per second to the database
options.explanation: Correct. Write-through writes the database synchronously on every update, so it does nothing to reduce database write volume.

options.text: Cache-aside with delete-on-write is the best fit here
options.explanation: Incorrect. Each increment would update the DB and delete the key, so the database still takes every write and the cache is constantly emptied.

options.text: The accepted loss window is roughly equal to the flush interval
options.explanation: Correct. Anything incremented since the last flush lives only in the cache, so a crash loses up to one interval's worth (unless the cache is replicated or persisted).

questions.workedExample:
1. Write volume: 30,000 updates a second to a single row. In Postgres each `UPDATE` takes a row lock, so they serialise and contend.
2. Write-back: `INCR article:9:views` in Redis (a constant-time in-memory operation), and a job every second reads the total and runs one `UPDATE`.
3. Database writes fall from tens of thousands a second to about one.
4. Risk: a crash loses whatever was incremented since the last successful flush, about one second of views here, which the scenario says is acceptable. Delayed or failed flushes widen that window.
5. Write-through and cache-aside both leave the database doing every write, so neither solves the problem.
6. Initialise counters from the durable total after cache loss and keep flush ordering idempotent: blindly writing a reset counter or replaying an old total can corrupt counts that were already saved.

questions.prompt: An orders service is considering **write-back** caching to cut write latency. Which of these are genuine consequences it must plan for? Select all that apply.

options.text: Acknowledged writes can be lost if a cache node fails before flushing
options.explanation: Correct. Until the flush, the only copy is in cache memory. Replication and an append-only log narrow this risk; without them, it is the defining risk of write-back.

options.text: Reports and other services that query the database directly will see data that lags behind the cache
options.explanation: Correct. With successful on-time flushes the delay is around one interval; failures or backlog can make it longer, so anything bypassing the cache reads old data.

options.text: Reads of recently written keys through the cache will miss
options.explanation: Incorrect. With write-back the cache has the newest value, so reads through it hit. It is readers of the *database* that see stale data.

options.text: Flush failures and ordering need explicit handling, for example retrying a batch that the database partly rejected
options.explanation: Correct. If a flushed write violates a constraint, the user was already told it succeeded. You need retry, dead-letter and conflict rules.

options.text: Write volume to the database rises, because every write is sent twice
options.explanation: Incorrect. Write-back usually *reduces* database writes by coalescing repeated updates into one flush.

questions.workedExample:
Walk through who holds the newest data:

1. Write arrives → cache updated → **ack**. Newest data: cache only.
2. Flush (later) → database updated. Newest data: both.

Between 1 and 2:
- A cache crash loses it (A true).
- Database readers see the old value (B true).
- Cache readers see the new value (C false).

At step 2 the database might reject the write, after the user was told it succeeded (D true). And coalescing means fewer database writes, not more (E false).

For orders, these risks are usually unacceptable, which is why write-back suits counters and analytics instead.

lessons.title: Refresh a hot entry before it expires
lessons.summary: Use an entry-age threshold to reload popular values in the background without refreshing every cold key.
lessons.body:
Expiry makes the next reader wait for a reload. Refresh-ahead uses a read near the end of an entry’s lifetime to start that work while the current copy is still available.

## Refresh-ahead

Another pattern tackles the miss that happens when a popular key expires. With **refresh-ahead**, the cache reloads an entry *before* it expires, once it has been read close to the end of its life. You choose a **refresh point**, often expressed as a **refresh factor**: a fraction of the TTL. With a 60-second TTL and a factor of 0.8, the refresh point is at 48 seconds.

A read before the refresh point is an ordinary hit. A read after it, but before expiry, still returns the current value immediately and also starts a background reload. Moving the refresh point earlier gives the reload more time to finish but refreshes more often; moving it close to expiry leaves little time for a slow reload.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: the office coffee jar
> When the office coffee jar is getting low, whoever makes a cup orders a new bag, but only if people are actually drinking it. Everyone keeps using the old jar until the delivery arrives, and a jar of decaf nobody touches is never reordered.
>
> **How it maps:** The jar is the cached entry, "getting low" is passing the refresh point, and making a cup is a read. That read triggers the reorder (background reload) but is still served from the existing jar. The untouched decaf is a cold key that is allowed to expire.
>
> **Where it stops:** A late delivery leaves an empty jar, just as a slow or failed reload can still let the entry expire and cause a miss. And old coffee is still the coffee you bought, whereas a cached copy can already be out of date compared with the database.

- Successful timely refreshes hide expiry for hot keys; slow or failed refreshes can still lead to a miss.
- Keys nobody reads near expiry are left to expire, so cold data is not refreshed for nothing.
- If the predictions are poor, you pay for reloads that nobody uses.

Caffeine's `refreshAfterWrite` is an example. The later early-refresh unit shows a probabilistic version that reduces stampede risk.

## Key takeaways
- The refresh factor sets the entry age at which a read starts background work.
- Earlier refreshes provide more time to finish but can perform work nobody uses.
- Only timely successful refreshes hide expiry; cold keys and failed refreshes can still miss.

## Further reading
- [Refresh — Caffeine documentation](https://github.com/ben-manes/caffeine/wiki/Refresh)
- [Caching best practices — AWS](https://aws.amazon.com/caching/best-practices/)

questions.prompt: A pricing service caches each product for 60 s using refresh-ahead with a refresh point at 48 s. A request for a hot product arrives 50 s after it was loaded. What happens?

options.text: The request waits while the cache reloads the value from the database
options.explanation: That is what happens after an entry has *expired*. Refresh-ahead exists precisely to avoid this wait for hot keys.

options.text: The request gets the current cached value straight away, and a background reload is started
options.explanation: Correct. The entry is past its refresh point but not expired, so the reader is served immediately and the reload happens asynchronously.

options.text: The request is a miss, because refresh-ahead deletes entries at the refresh point
